title: A deformed grid: where does the coordinate system stretch or fold?
summary: A regular grid is pushed through a map. The bent grid shows, at a glance, where cells are squeezed, stretched, sheared or folded over. The original grid is kept faint underneath as a reference.

media.alt: A square grid drawn faintly in blue, over it the same lines mapped into wavy teal horizontal lines and orange vertical lines forming a curved grid of quadrilaterals, with equal axis scales.
media.caption: Reference render of class F2.2 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Where does the coordinate system stretch or fold?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y in the plane, equal scale, -1.3 to 1.3. Pale blue: the original grid, 11 lines each way on [-1, 1]. Teal: images of the original horizontal lines (y = const). Amber: images of the original vertical lines (x = const).
look_at: Where are the cells closest together, and where far apart?
Do any lines cross each other? Crossing lines mean a fold. Here they never cross.
Compare each deformed corner of the square with its original corner: which way did it move?
Do the two families of lines stay roughly perpendicular, or are they sheared?
as_drawn: The map is (x, y) goes to (x + 0.25 sin 2.5y, y + 0.25 sin 2.5x). Its corner (1, 1) moves to (1.15, 1.15) and (-1, 1) moves to (-0.85, 0.85).
The determinant is 1 - 0.39 cos(2.5x) cos(2.5y): it ranges from 0.61 to 1.31 on the square. It is positive everywhere, so there is nothing to mark as a fold.
The original grid is ghosted as the standard asks. 'Fold locations marked' holds vacuously: no folds exist, which is a finding of the plot.
read_the_figure.proves: The qualitative pattern of stretch, squeeze and shear, and the absence of folds at this grid resolution. It does not prove the map has no fold between grid lines or outside the square.
if_wrong: The original grid missing: you cannot tell what changed.
Lines overlapping and drawn identically: a fold is hidden in a dense patch.
Unequal axes: shear and stretch cannot be told apart.

terms.meaning: Lines of constant u or constant v in the domain; their images are curves in the image.
A smooth change of shape described by a map.
Local lengthening or shortening of a grid line segment.
A change of angle between the two families of lines.
A place where the map reverses orientation: lines of one family cross back over themselves; the Jacobian determinant passes through zero.
A light copy of the original drawn beneath for reference.

remember: Crossing lines of one family means a fold: det J = 0 there.
Cell area ratio equals det J.
Equal axis scales. Mark folds where they occur.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Lines are the marks. Colour distinguishes the two families (teal for lines of constant y, amber for lines of constant x) so the reader can follow each direction. The pale blue grid behind is the unchanged reference. Position is the plane.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A coordinate system is a way of labelling points; a map re-labels or moves them. A grid makes both visible, and the bend of each line shows the local direction of stretch. The change in size of a cell, relative to the ghost, is the local area factor, det J. Where a family of lines would cross itself, the map folds.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A grid line spacing that is too coarse can step over a fold narrower than the spacing. Lines drawn in one colour can hide a fold in a dense region. The eye overestimates stretch in the direction of line density and misjudges area. And a reflection leaves a grid that looks undeformed: only the colour order of the families reveals it.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: The ghosted original tells you what 'deformed' means. A fold marker, computed from det J = 0, tells you where the map is not invertible. In this render none exists; the empty list is itself information, but it should be stated.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Use a determinant heat map (F2.3) when the question is magnitude, a displacement field (F2.4) when the deformation is small, and a before-and-after region (F2.1) when identity of points matters.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Colour each cell by its determinant (a diverging map centred on 1) to put the number on the picture, and draw the det J = 0 contour as a thick line if it exists.

steps.title: The Jacobian and cell area
steps.note: Each factor 0.625 is 0.25 times 2.5. Over [-1, 1]^2 the determinant runs from 0.61 (at the centre, cells squeezed to 61 percent of their area) to 1.31 (at the middles of the four edges, (0, plus or minus 1) and (plus or minus 1, 0), where cells are enlarged); the corners sit at 0.75.

steps.title: When would it fold?
steps.note: For amplitude a = 0.25 there is no fold; at a = 0.4 the centre cell collapses, and beyond that the grid lines cross and a fold appears.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) where is the grid most squeezed? (2) Is there a fold? (3) Where did the corner (1, 1) go?

solution.text: Near the centre, where the teal lines bunch together and the amber lines bunch together: det J = 0.61 at the origin.
No: no two lines of the same family cross, and det J never drops below 0.61. A fold needs det J = 0.
The corner (1, 1) maps to (1 + 0.25 sin 2.5, 1 + 0.25 sin 2.5), that is (1.15, 1.15).

worked.answer: Squeezed to 61 percent of the original area at the centre, enlarged to 131 percent at the middles of the edges, and no fold.

analyze.q: How would the grid look if the amplitude 0.25 were raised to 0.5?
analyze.hint: Where does det J first reach zero?

analyze.q: A map reflects the square in the line y = x. What does the deformed grid look like and how can you still tell?
Why is a ghost grid more valuable here than a legend?

evaluate.q: A grid with 6 lines looks smooth, one with 60 shows a fold. What does that say about checking maps with plots?

create: Raise the amplitude to 0.4 and 0.5 and mark the fold curve det J = 0 on top of the deformed grid.
Colour each cell by log of its area ratio.

checks.q: What distinguishes a fold from a mere strong stretch on a deformed grid?
checks.hint: Look at lines of one family.
checks.answer: In a fold lines of the same family cross over each other and the orientation flips (det J changes sign). A stretch keeps order.

checks.q: Cells at the centre have area 0.61 of the original. By what factor are their sides squeezed on average?
The deformed grid shows no crossing lines. Is the map guaranteed to be one-to-one over the square?
checks.answer: No: a fold narrower than the line spacing could be missed, and the Jacobian only gives local invertibility. Check det J on a fine grid and the global map.
